Tab-completion offers `on`, `off`, `status`, `toggle` (`src/orchestrator.ts:84-88`).

**Actions** (`src/orchestrator.ts:89-109`): empty args → `toggle`; `on`/`off`/`toggle` → `setEnabled`; `status` → report; anything else → usage error. **Footer status indicator** (`setStatus("orchestrator", ...)`, `:61-63`):
- Enabled + available → `theme.fg("accent", "orchestrator")` (word "orchestrator" in accent color)
- Otherwise → `undefined` (hidden)

**Notifications** (`ctx.ui.notify(msg, level)`, levels `info|warning|error`):

| Trigger | Message | Level |
|---|---|---|
| `on`/`toggle`→enabled | `Orchestrator mode enabled.` | info |
| `off` | `Orchestrator mode disabled.` | info |
| Enable while unavailable (child Pi, outside Herdr, no spawn_pi) | `Orchestrator mode requires a Herdr Parent with spawn_pi active.` | warning |
| Enable with invalid config | `Invalid config at <path>: <error>. Orchestrator mode is disabled and spawn_pi is blocked.` | warning |

Investigation complete. The checkout is `pi-herdr-subagents` (branch `status-appearance`, clean tree). Below are the CLI/TUI visual conventions found, all in the extension's display layer.

## 1. Findings — visual conventions that can inform orchestrator output

**Colors — semantic Theme palette only, no raw ANSI.** All colored output routes through pi's `Theme.fg(ThemeColor, text)`:
- `accent` = in-progress/working; `success` = complete; `warning` = needs-input; `error` = failed (tools.ts:280–285)
- `toolTitle` = tool name + task IDs (tools.ts:92, 195); `toolOutput` = child summaries (tools.ts:201); `muted` = all metadata (role badges, failure reasons, locations, model/thinking/session) (tools.ts:195–213)
- The only other colors used are `accent` for the status-bar label (orchestrator.ts:39) and `toolTitle`/`accent` in the renderCall header (tools.ts:88–95). The full palette (from pi 0.84.1 `ThemeColor` type, e.g. `border`, `borderAccent`, `dim`, `warning`) is available but unused — flat text, no borders.

**Glyphs — a fixed 4-state icon set** (tools.ts:272–276): `◌` working, `✓` complete, `!` needs input, `×` incomplete. Note `×` is U+00D7, not `✗`; needs-input is `!`, not `⚠`.

**Compact status patterns** — the key reusable patterns:
- Live progress header: `working · 2 of 5 settled` (tools.ts:112, 176–178); plain-text echo: `spawn_pi: working · 1 of 3 settled`
- Final batch header: `✓ 2 of 2 tasks complete` / mixed: `× incomplete · 1 of 3 complete` / blocked: `! needs input · 1 of 2 complete` (tools.ts:257–260, 214–226 for state derivation)
- Per-child row: `✓ task-1 [explore]` — icon + taskId + muted `[role]` badge; non-complete rows append a state label and `·`-separated facts: `! task-2 [reviewer] needs input · tab-5/pane-2`; failures get a terse reason: `× task-3 incomplete · model unavailable` (tools.ts:195–196, 148–175)
- `·` (U+00B7) is the universal field separator; `:` appears only for the needs-input error message
- Failure reasons are single-token-ish phrases: "role not found", "model unavailable", "could not start", "prompt failed", "result unreadable", "parent stopped waiting" (tools.ts:148–175)

**Panels — none; flat rows by design.** No box-drawing/panel characters anywhere in `src/` (grep for `│┌└├─╭╮╰╯═█░` returns only `Type` imports). The result card is one `Text` block of `\n`-joined lines (tools.ts:116–118), collapsed by default, with an expanded mode adding indented muted detail lines: summary (`toolOutput`), `summary truncated`, error message, `location:`, `model:`, `thinking:`, `model selection:`, `thinking selection:`, `session:` (tools.ts:198–214).

**Status-bar / footer indicator:** `ctx.ui.setStatus("orchestrator", theme.fg("accent", "orchestrator"))` shown while enabled, cleared otherwise (orchestrator.ts:39); toggles announce via `ctx.ui.notify(msg, "info" | "warning" | "error")` (orchestrator.ts:47–48, 55, 64–65, 72).

**Unrelated but adjacent convention:** child/parent Herdr tab+pane names `Pi [<parent-label>] task-N` / `Pi [<parent-label>]` (host.ts:212–215, 455–465), sanitized to lowercase alnum-dash; role text is control-char-stripped before rendering (tools.ts:263–270) — untrusted input is never echoed raw into the TUI.

## 2. Evidence

- `src/tools.ts` — renderResult/renderChild/summarize/stateIcon/stateColor/shortReason: lines 88–118, 148–175, 176–193, 194–214, 214–226, 253–285
- `src/orchestrator.ts` — status bar + notify usage: lines 39, 47–48, 55–58, 64–65, 72
- `src/batch.ts` — progress snapshot/counter feeding the live header: lines 79–97 (`completed of total`)
- `src/herdr/host.ts` — naming conventions: lines 212–215, 220–224, 455–473
- `test/unit/tools.test.ts` — golden assertions locking the exact glyph/format patterns: lines 104–106, 147–154, 176–178, 234–237 (e.g. `/^working · 1 of 3 settled/`, `/◌ task-1 \[explore \[31m\] working/` proving sanitization)
- Palette: `ThemeColor` union in `@earendil-works/pi-coding-agent` dist theme types (pi 0.84.1)

## 3. Connections

`batch.ts` (ConcurrentBatchRunner) owns settlement accounting → emits `BatchProgress {completed,total,results}` → `tools.ts` `renderResult` maps it to the live `working · N of M settled` header and per-task rows keyed by `requestIndex` in request order. On finish, `SpawnBatchResult` flows through `batchDisplayState` (complete/needs_input/incomplete derivation at tools.ts:214–226) into the icon+aggregate header; collapsed vs expanded (`expanded` flag from the UI) controls whether child summaries/model/thinking details are emitted. Plain-text fallbacks (`summarize`, `summarizeProgress`) mirror the same icons and separators for non-TUI consumers. The orchestrator command is display-independent except the `accent` status label and notify severities.

## 4. Gaps

- I did not run `pnpm test` (would require install; read-only role) — format/icon claims are verified against the golden test assertions instead.
- The `Text` component API from `@earendil-works/pi-tui` is used only as `new Text(string, 0, 0)`; no wrapping/panel options are exercised, so I can't report on those capabilities.
- Recent commits (e.g. "feat(orchestrator): show roles in status", branch `status-appearance`) touch `orchestrator.ts` status — worth checking the diff if the Parent plans to extend the orchestrator status label further.
- No interference observed: working tree clean, single checkout, no concurrent edits detected during inspection.

# pi-herdr-subagents

An expert-pilot [Pi](https://pi.dev) package that adds `spawn_pi`: one call starts 1–8 fresh, visible Pi sessions in the current Herdr workspace and collects attributed final answers from their session JSONL files.

## Install

```bash
pi install /path/to/pi-herdr-subagents
```

The package loads safely outside Herdr. Calling `spawn_pi` there returns an actionable unavailable result instead of crashing Pi.

## Use

Ask Parent Pi to call `spawn_pi` with independent tasks. Each task defaults to its own no-focus tab; use `placement: "split"` for a sibling split. The live result card shows every task in request order as `working`, `complete`, `needs input`, or `incomplete`; requested roles appear as visible row badges, while runtime details appear only when expanded.

### Orchestrator mode

Use `/orchestrator` to toggle a Parent mode that proactively delegates useful bounded exploration, independent implementation, and review while retaining responsibility for synthesis and final verification. Explicit forms are `/orchestrator on`, `/orchestrator off`, and `/orchestrator status`. A footer indicator is shown while the mode is enabled.

Orchestrator state is session-wide and survives resume, reload, and tree navigation. Fresh sessions use `orchestrator.enabled` from `~/.pi/agent/herdr-subagents.json`; forks inherit the source session's current state. Missing configuration defaults to disabled. Child Pis and Pi sessions outside Herdr cannot enable the mode.

### Child roles and runtime defaults

Copy the shipped global config and role catalogue, then customize them:

```bash
cp herdr-subagents.example.json ~/.pi/agent/herdr-subagents.json
cp -R herdr-subagents.example ~/.pi/agent/herdr-subagents
```

The global config contains only Orchestrator and runtime defaults:

```json
{
  "orchestrator": { "enabled": false },
  "defaults": {
    "model": ["openai-codex/gpt-5.6-luna", "openai-codex/gpt-5.6-sol"],
    "thinking": "medium"
  }
}
```

Each role is a Markdown document in `~/.pi/agent/herdr-subagents/roles/`; direct `.md` symlinks, such as those created by Home Manager, are supported. Its filename stem is the case-sensitive role name. Put optional `description`, `model`, and `thinking` metadata in YAML frontmatter; the trimmed document body is the appended identity prompt:

```md
---
description: Read-only codebase reconnaissance and evidence gathering.
model:
  - openai-codex/gpt-5.6-luna
  - openai-codex/gpt-5.6-sol
thinking: low
---

Act as a read-only repository investigator.

Locate the relevant entry points, trace important control flow, and cite file
paths and line ranges. Do not modify files.
```

Tasks can set `role`, `model`, and `thinking`. Model and thinking resolve independently: task override, role, configured default, then Parent setting. Config `defaults.model` and role frontmatter `model` accept either one exact `provider/model-id` string or a non-empty ordered array of them (model IDs may contain `/`). The selected config layer is tried in order against available models; if none is available, the task fails rather than falling through to a lower-precedence layer. Task overrides remain a single string, and inherited Parent models are not availability-validated. A role supplies only an appended identity prompt; it does not replace Pi's system prompt, tools, or project context. The configured role descriptions are visible to Parent Pi, but role prompts and model mappings are not.

This replaces the former JSON `roles` property. Move each old `roles.<name>` entry to `herdr-subagents/roles/<name>.md`, put `description`, `model`, and `thinking` in frontmatter, put `prompt` in the body, and remove `roles` from the JSON file. Inline JSON roles are rejected; there is no automated migration command.

Configuration is loaded when the extension loads. Run `/reload` after editing either the JSON config or a role document to apply changes to future fresh sessions; it does not reset the current session's Orchestrator state. Invalid configuration disables Orchestrator mode with a warning and blocks a batch before Herdr is inspected.

Role prompts must not contain secrets. The extension writes the literal Child role instruction heading and prompt to a private temporary file, then passes that file to Pi; prompt contents are not placed in process arguments.

At session start, the extension generates and stores a short internal Parent label (for example, `amber-finch`). The Parent tab is renamed `Pi [<parent>]`; each child tab, pane, and Pi session is named `Pi [<parent>] task-N` (for example, `Pi [amber-finch] task-1`). The label is unrelated to the Parent Pi's `/name` and does not affect the `/resume` list. This keeps children from concurrent Parent Pis distinguishable. Successful results include a child session ID. Closing the child pane does **not** delete that session; resume it with:

```bash
pi --session <id>
# or use /resume in Pi
```

## Important pilot limitation

All children work in the Parent Pi's current checkout concurrently. They can overwrite or invalidate each other's edits, observe changing files, and interfere through tests or Git operations. This package does no locking, write detection, reconciliation, rollback, persistence, or background collection. Review the final checkout yourself.

Blocked, failed, interrupted, and unattributable children are deliberately left visible in Herdr for inspection while the Parent session remains active. Parent abort stops collection only; it does not interrupt or close accepted children. When the Parent Pi exits or switches to a new, resumed, or forked session, the extension closes still-open child panes it created after verifying their occupants. `/reload` does not close children.

## Development

With [devenv](https://devenv.sh/) installed, enter the Node.js 22 development shell:

```bash
devenv shell
pnpm install
```

## Option A — Aggregate state, icon-only rows **(recommended)**

```text
spawn_pi  2 tasks
✓ 2 of 2 tasks complete
  ✓ task-1  [explore]
  ✓ task-2  [explore]
```

Each fact appears once: the header says the batch completed; row icons show which tasks succeeded. Keeps task attribution visible and scans well.

**Mixed result**

```text
spawn_pi  2 tasks
! 1 complete · 1 needs input
  ✓ task-1  [explore]
  ! task-2  [reviewer]  needs input
```

Only exceptional rows need a text label.

---

## Option B — Outcome sentence, neutral rows

```text
spawn_pi  2 tasks
Completed 2 of 2 tasks
  task-1  [explore]
  task-2  [explore]
```

The calmest presentation. Removes all repeated success markers, but individual rows no longer visually confirm their outcome.

---

## Option C — Rows are the result; drop the aggregate status

```text
spawn_pi  2 tasks
✓ task-1  [explore]
✓ task-2  [explore]
```

Smallest fully attributed card. The call title already says there are two tasks, so the two checked rows imply `2 of 2`. Less convenient for batches of 6–8 or mixed results.

---

## Option D — One-line collapsed result

```text
spawn_pi  2 tasks
✓ 2 of 2 tasks complete  ›
```

Expanded:

```text
✓ 2 of 2 tasks complete  ⌄
  task-1  [explore]
  task-2  [explore]
```

Best for transcript density. Task attribution is hidden until expansion, which changes the current always-visible policy.

---

### Recommendation

Use **Option A**: preserve the stable per-task rows, remove the word `complete` from successful rows, and phrase the aggregate as one natural status. It is the smallest behavior change and remains clear for partial or mixed outcomes.

surfaces.title: Where complexity lives—and whether the seams hold

surfaces.markdown:
# Architecture at a glance

The key distinction is **contained complexity** versus **scattered complexity**. `HerdrChildHost` is large because it hides a difficult external lifecycle; `tools.ts` is concerning because unrelated presentation and execution responsibilities accumulate in one place.

## How to read this

- 🟢 **Deep modules:** `ChildHost → HerdrChildHost` and `ChildResultReader → JsonlChildResultReader` expose small interfaces while hiding substantial implementation complexity.
- 🔵 **Behavioral center:** `ConcurrentBatchRunner` coordinates routing, starting, prompting, reading, and closing without knowing socket or JSONL details.
- 🟣 **Refactoring target:** `tools.ts` combines schema, execution adaptation, summaries, runtime guards, sanitization, and TUI rendering.
- The arrows form a **directed acyclic graph**—there are no import cycles.

## Practical conclusion

| Area | Complexity | Seam quality | Action |
|---|---:|---:|---|
| `herdr/host.ts` | Highest operational | Strong | Keep intact unless lifecycle concerns change independently |
| `tools.ts` | Highest accidental | Weakest | Separate pure presentation from registration/execution |
| `batch.ts` | High behavioral | Strong | Keep as orchestration center |
| `results.ts` | Dense algorithmic | Strong | Preserve narrow reader interface |
| `model-routing.ts` | Branch-heavy policy | Mostly clear | Centralize duplicated model/thinking validation |

### Suggested order

1. Split presentation logic out of `tools.ts`.
2. Give the task-marker contract one owner.
3. Consolidate shared model/thinking validation.
4. Only create a shared JSONL parser if it preserves each consumer’s distinct rules.

**Overall:** the architecture is healthy at the large scale, but several small duplicated contracts reduce seam clarity—about **7/10**.

A **Share** is an immutable, unlisted public snapshot of one owned Activity on one Library Entry.

## API

```text
POST   /v1/library/entries/{entryId}/activities/{activityId}/shares
GET    /v1/library/entries/{entryId}/shares

```

Creation uses `Idempotency-Key` and a client-supplied IANA timezone. The API snapshots the Diversion ID/kind/title/subtitle, Activity State and occurrence instant, and the derived local calendar date.

## Public pages

```text
GET /shares/{randomToken}
GET /shares/{randomToken}/card.png
```

The existing Go site server-renders the page and Open Graph metadata. The card is a generated 1200×630 PNG with a bold social gradient, text, and Diversions branding—no third-party artwork or creator identity.

Example: **Dune — Finished** · Book · Frank Herbert · August 5, 2026.

- Any Activity may be shared and may have multiple Shares.
- Same idempotency key/request replays the original Share; mismatches conflict.
- Revocation hides the Share, makes public routes return `404`, and retains the row privately for idempotency.
- Entry or user deletion permanently cascades all Shares.
- No expiration, public JSON, analytics, native deep links, rate limit, or active-Share cap.

## Accepted risks

- TMDB-derived metadata is persisted without attribution despite published attribution/cache terms.
- Anyone with the URL may reshare it.
- Social caches may retain previews after revocation.
- Infrastructure logs may observe unlisted URLs; application logs should redact tokens where practical.

# Share diversion progress — confirmed design

## Product contract

- A **Share** is an immutable public snapshot of one owned **Activity** on one **Library Entry**.
- Any current or historical Activity may be shared.
- An Activity can produce multiple Shares; transport retries are deduplicated with `Idempotency-Key`.
- Snapshot: Entry/Activity/Diversion IDs, kind, title, optional subtitle, Activity State, occurrence instant, and a calendar date derived from a client-supplied IANA timezone.
- No artwork or creator identity in v1. Ratings/reviews are deferred until their domain feature exists.
- Shares are unlisted, unauthenticated, non-indexed, and remain active until revoked or their Entry/user is deleted.

## Authenticated API

```text
POST   /v1/library/entries/{entryId}/activities/{activityId}/shares
GET    /v1/library/entries/{entryId}/shares
DELETE /v1/library/shares/{shareId}
```

Creation uses `Idempotency-Key` plus `{ "timezone": "America/Chicago" }`. Create/list responses include the private Share UUID, source IDs, immutable snapshot, full configured public URL, and timestamps. Lists are active-only, newest-first, and cursor-paginated.

## Public web contract

```text
GET /shares/{randomToken}
GET /shares/{randomToken}/card.png
```

- Existing Go site server-renders HTML and Open Graph/Twitter metadata.
- Card: generated 1200×630 PNG, bold social gradient, no third-party artwork.
- Title-first copy, e.g. **Dune — Finished**, followed by kind/subtitle and **August 5, 2026**.
- Presentation maps persisted `abandoned` to **Stopped**.
- No public JSON, analytics, expiration, native deep link, or direct social integration.
- Clients invoke the native/browser share sheet.

## Lifecycle

Revocation sets `revokedAt`, removes the Share from active lists, and makes public routes return `404`. The row remains privately for idempotency and cannot be restored. A new key may create a new Share. Entry or Clerk-user deletion permanently cascades active and revoked Shares.

## Explicitly accepted risks

- TMDB-derived metadata is persisted without attribution despite published attribution/cache terms.
- No creation rate limit or active-Share cap.
- Anyone possessing the URL may reshare it.
- Social-platform caches cannot be purged reliably after revocation.
- Infrastructure logs may observe unlisted URLs; application logs should redact tokens where practical.

## How to read these graphs

Arrows point from a prerequisite to the task that depends on it. The validation graph uses a fan-out/fan-in shape: formatting and generation happen first, independent checks run in parallel, and the build waits for all three checks.

`dev-deps-reset` reuses `dev-deps-down` before deleting local PostgreSQL/Redis state and recreating both services. The Redis reset task remains imperative because it must safely coexist with an already-running Redis process.

### API process dependencies

The API process waits for both PostgreSQL and Redis. This dependency is owned by the devenv process definition; `run` starts the API with live reload.

## Decision

Make lifecycle events the only persisted source of lifecycle state.

- `entries` stores identity and generic timestamps, but no lifecycle state.
- Each event records one state established at one time.
- A per-entry sequence defines causal order.
- Entry reads derive lifecycle state and state-change time from the newest event.
- Public history exposes state events rather than reconstructed transitions.

This is deliberately not a full event-sourcing framework. It is one append-only history owned by the Library Entry repository.

surfaces.mermaid:
flowchart LR
  subgraph EntryTable[entries]
    E[Entry identity and metadata]
  end
  subgraph EventTable[lifecycle_events]
    E1[Sequence 1 state queued]
    E2[Sequence 2 state in progress]
    E3[Sequence 3 state finished]
    E1 --> E2 --> E3
  end
  E --> E1
  READ[Get or List entry] -->|latest event| E3
  HIST[List history] -->|all events by sequence| E1
  WRITE[Transition] -->|append only| E3

surfaces.markdown:
## Persistence model

```sql
CREATE TABLE diversions.lifecycle_events (
    entry_id   uuid        NOT NULL
        REFERENCES diversions.entries(id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
    sequence   bigint      NOT NULL CHECK (sequence > 0),
    state      text        NOT NULL CHECK (
        state IN ('queued', 'in_progress', 'finished', 'abandoned', 'paused')
    ),
    occurred_at timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT clock_timestamp(),
    PRIMARY KEY (entry_id, sequence)
);
```

Remove:

- `entries.lifecycle_state`
- `lifecycle_events.id`
- `lifecycle_events.from_state`
- `lifecycle_events.to_state`
- the timestamp and UUID ordering index

The composite primary key is sufficient for ascending history scans and backward latest-event scans. There is no public or domain need for a globally addressable event ID.

## Domain types

```go
type Entry struct {
    ID                      uuid.UUID
    UserID                  string
    Diversion               catalog.DiversionRef
    CollectionIDs           []uuid.UUID
    LifecycleState          LifecycleState // derived from newest event
    LifecycleStateChangedAt time.Time      // newest event occurred_at
    Title                   string
    Subtitle                string
    ImageURL                 string
    CreatedAt               time.Time
    UpdatedAt               time.Time      // generic entry mutation time
}

type LifecycleEvent struct {
    State      LifecycleState
    OccurredAt time.Time
}
```

Event sequence and entry ID remain persistence details. Callers already scope history by entry, and history is returned in canonical order.

surfaces.mermaid:
sequenceDiagram
  participant API
  participant Repo as Entry repository
  participant Entry as entries
  participant Events as lifecycle events

  API->>Repo: Transition to finished
  Repo->>Entry: Lock owned entry row
  Repo->>Events: Read newest sequence and state
  alt State already finished
    Repo-->>API: Return current entry with no writes
  else State differs
    Repo->>Events: Insert next sequence and finished
    Repo->>Entry: Update generic updated time
    Repo-->>API: Return entry with derived lifecycle
  end

surfaces.markdown:
## Query shape and performance

- **Get by ID or Diversion:** join one latest event using `ORDER BY sequence DESC LIMIT 1`.
- **List entries:** select the page of at most 101 entries first, then perform the latest-event lookup only for that page.
- **History:** scan the composite primary key in ascending sequence order.
- **Transition:** lock the entry row before reading the latest event and allocating `sequence + 1`.

Do not use `LAG`. The public DTO is a raw state event, so no previous state needs to be reconstructed.

The row lock serializes concurrent transitions. `PRIMARY KEY (entry_id, sequence)` is the database backstop against duplicate sequence allocation.

steps.detail: Require one or more events per entry, valid from and to chains, and latest to_state equal to entries.lifecycle_state.

steps.label: Backfill sequence
steps.detail: Assign row_number per entry ordered by existing created_at and id.

steps.label: Reshape events
steps.detail: Rename to_state to state and created_at to occurred_at; remove from_state and global event id; add the composite primary key.

steps.label: Remove entry state
steps.detail: Drop entries.lifecycle_state after the audit succeeds.

steps.label: Regenerate and adapt
steps.detail: Update sqlc queries, repository mapping, domain types, API outputs, smoke tests, and generated code.

steps.label: Verify concurrency
steps.detail: Prove initial event atomicity, same-state no-op, contiguous sequences, concurrent serialization, and derived get and list results against PostgreSQL.

surfaces.markdown:
## Explicit trade-offs

- PostgreSQL cannot declaratively guarantee that every entry has an initial event without a pointer or trigger. Creation remains a deep transactional repository operation and is covered by integration tests.
- Privileged direct SQL can still alter history. No update or delete event queries are exposed; stronger privilege or stored-function architecture is deferred until there is a real operational need.
- History remains unpaginated. If that changes, an opaque cursor can encode sequence without adding sequence to the DTO.

```text
│   ├── entries/
│   │   ├── model.go              # modify — collection IDs and list metadata
│   │   ├── service.go            # modify — save/attach/unlink behavior

│   │   ├── routes.go             # modify — replace move route
│   │   ├── routes_test.go        # modify — new route contract
│   │   └── outputs_test.go       # modify — new JSON shape
```

- [ ] Saving Arrival into two collections returns the same entry ID.
- [ ] Only one initial lifecycle event is created.
- [ ] Lifecycle transitions appear identically through both collections.
- [ ] Unlinking one collection preserves the other membership.
- [ ] Unlinking the final membership preserves the entry and history.
- [ ] Deleting a collection preserves its formerly linked entries.
- [ ] Deleting the shared entry removes every membership and lifecycle event.
- [ ] Concurrent saves cannot create duplicate entries.
- [ ] Collection listing paginates by membership creation time.
- [ ] Cross-user memberships are rejected by database constraints.

| Layer | What | How |
|---|---|---|

| Repository | Uniqueness, cascades, transactions, concurrent saves, ordering | Existing PostgreSQL integration test harness |
| Transport | New routes, request validation, output shapes and status codes | Huma route and serialization tests |
| Generated code | Migration/query consistency | `just generate-check` and `just agent-validate` |

| Risk | Impact | Mitigation |
|---|---|---|

| Cross-user memberships are inserted | Tenant data corruption | Composite user-scoped foreign keys |

| Chose | Over | Because |
|---|---|---|

| One shared entry | Separate entries sharing lifecycle | One owner for lifecycle, history, and deletion |
| Explicit attach/unlink | Retaining “move” | Multi-collection membership makes move incorrect |
| Keep unfiled entries | Delete after final unlink | Organization should not imply library deletion |

None.

    participant S as Catalog search service
    participant O as Open Library provider
    participant OL as Open Library API

    C->>A: GET search with query, book kind, language, and Bearer token
    A->>A: Clerk middleware authenticates request
    A->>S: Search with query, book kind, and language
    S->>S: Trim query and validate minimum length
    S->>S: Validate that book has one source owner
    S->>O: Search for the requested book kind
    O->>O: Build query with page 1 and limit 20
    O->>O: Convert en-US language to en
    O->>OL: GET search.json

surfaces.markdown:
### What makes this specifically a book search?

- `kind=book` routes the request only to the **book** source, owned by the Open Library provider.
- The provider asks Open Library for up to **20** matches and skips entries without a usable edition ID (`OL…M`).
- Each result gets a stable, provider-qualified ID such as `openlibrary:book:OL3567303M`, plus title, authors as subtitle, cover URL, and first publish date.
- `language=en-US` becomes Open Library's `lang=en` filter.

### Validation and failures

| Point | Result |
|---|---|
| Missing/invalid Bearer token | Auth middleware rejects the request |
| Query shorter than 2 runes | `400` invalid request |
| Unsupported or repeated kind | `400` invalid request |
| Open Library rate limit | Catalog rate-limit error |
| Provider/network failure | Catalog unavailable error |

### Follow the selected result

Use its ID in `GET /v1/books/openlibrary:book:OL3567303M`. The book service reads its 24-hour, 1,000-entry LRU cache first; on a miss it fetches the Open Library edition, authors, and (when needed) work description.

**Verdict: strong overall conformance.** I found **no critical or high-severity ownership/dependency violations**. The package layout expresses the intended product boundaries, and framework/vendor/generated types stay behind the expected seams.

| Result | Count |
|---|---:|
| Major architecture violations | **0** |
| Medium discrepancies | **2** |

> Scope: current working tree, including staged changes. This was read-only review work; no source files were changed.

surfaces.markdown:
## Skill conformance matrix

| Review question | Result | Evidence |
|---|---|---|
| Services testable without Huma/HTTP | ✅ | Services depend on `notes.Repository`, `catalog.SearchProvider`, or `screen.Provider`; no Huma imports in service files. |
| Handlers translate rather than decide | ✅ | Notes, search, and screen handlers map input/output and errors; behavior remains in services/providers. |
| No sqlc/TMDB leakage into domain or public responses | ✅ | sqlc imports stop at `notes/repository.go` and app wiring; TMDB imports stay under `catalog/screen/tmdb`. |
| Modules register their operations | ✅ | `notes/api/routes.go`, `catalog/search/api/api.go`, and `catalog/screen/api/routes.go`. |
| Router/Huma adapter centralized | ✅ | `internal/app/server.go:30-73`; `humachi.New` appears in app assembly. |
| Goose migrations are schema truth | ✅ | `sqlc.yaml:4-9` points schema to migrations, queries to SQL sources, output to generated sqlc. |
| Generated files protected | ✅ | CI regenerates and diffs generated code (`.github/workflows/ci.yml:29-32`). Current generation has no drift. |
| Shared code truly neutral | ✅ | No `internal/shared` dumping ground; catalog-wide transport errors have a clear catalog owner. |
| Only currently useful abstractions | ⚠️ | The notes repository exposes one unused, unscoped lookup capability. |
| Tests target actual risk | ❌ | Catalog has focused tests; notes persistence/auth/server seams have none. |

## Discrepancy 1 — unscoped capability in the notes repository

**Severity: Medium · confirmed architecture discrepancy**

`internal/modules/notes/repository.go:15-33` exposes and implements:

```go
FindByID(ctx context.Context, id uuid.UUID) (Note, error)
```

But every notes use case is user-scoped. `internal/modules/notes/service.go:31-65` calls `FindByIDAndUser`, `ListByUser`, `Create`, `Update`, and `Delete`; it never calls `FindByID`. The corresponding unscoped `GetNote` SQL query is likewise not used by a service.

**Why this conflicts with the skill/project rules**
- Repository interfaces should be narrow and consumer-owned.
- Notes use cases are explicitly user-scoped.
- An unused unscoped read creates a future ownership/auth bypass path even though current handlers are safe.

**Suggested future correction:** remove the unused interface method, concrete method, and SQL query if no administrative use case owns them. Do not add an admin abstraction merely to justify the method.

Related minor orphan: `internal/modules/notes/errors.go:7` declares unused `ErrNotOwner`.

## Discrepancy 2 — test topology does not cover the risk-bearing seams

**Severity: Medium · confirmed testing/architecture discrepancy**

There are **zero test files** under:
- `internal/modules/notes`
- `internal/modules/notes/api`
- `internal/platform/auth`
- `internal/platform/db`
- `internal/app`

This leaves these architectural contracts unverified:

1. **Notes service behavior** without HTTP.
2. **SQLRepository behavior** against real PostgreSQL, including user scoping and `pgx.ErrNoRows → notes.ErrNotFound` mapping.
3. **Goose migration from an empty database**.
4. **Notes route/input/output/error behavior**.
5. **Group-level auth policy**, bearer security declaration, and public `/healthz` behavior.

Catalog test placement is much better: service, provider adapter, error mapping, route registration, cancellation, and timeout behavior all have focused tests.

**Suggested future order:**
1. Repository integration tests for cross-user isolation and not-found mapping.
2. Server/auth transport tests proving `/healthz` public and `/v1/*` protected.
3. Notes service and API tests.
4. Empty-database migration test.

## Watch item — future catalog kinds are predeclared

**Severity: Low · not currently harmful**

`internal/modules/catalog/model.go:12-14` defines book, video-game, and board-game kinds before sibling capabilities exist. The current screen provider rejects them.

This slightly exceeds the skill’s “current needs only” preference, but the project guidance explicitly anticipates these sibling capabilities and assigns kind ownership to `catalog`. Treat this as a watch item, **not a restructuring recommendation**. Revisit only if these constants begin creating misleading public contracts or conditional logic.

## What is already architecturally strong

- **Thin executable:** `cmd/api/main.go` only loads config, owns process signals, and calls `app.Run`.
- **Clear composition root:** `internal/app/app.go` constructs pool, sqlc queries, repositories, services, TMDB provider, readiness, router, and lifecycle.
- **Explicit auth policy:** `internal/app/server.go:64-73` applies auth per Huma group; `/healthz` remains a public Chi route.
- **Correct module map:** `notes`, `catalog/search`, and `catalog/screen` match project terminology and ownership.
- **Vendor locality:** TMDB lives under `internal/modules/catalog/screen/tmdb`; substantial conversion is in `mapper.go`; `NewProvider` returns concrete `*Provider`.
- **Shared catalog behavior has a real owner:** `internal/modules/catalog/api/errors.go` centralizes catalog HTTP error mapping.
- **Persistence flow conforms:** goose migration → sqlc sources/generated package → notes adapter → notes service → Huma handler.
- **No premature shared package:** no domain-neutral dumping ground was introduced.
- **Deployment/public artifact conventions:** runtime assets are under `deployments`; root `api/` is not misused for runtime handlers.
- **Automation:** CI checks format, generated-code drift, tests, vet, build, and Docker build.

## Verification performed

- Enumerated repository files/directories and Go packages.
- Reviewed app entry/assembly/router/lifecycle/config, all module boundaries, notes persistence flow, auth, sqlc/goose configuration, CI, and representative tests/adapters.
- Scanned dependency boundaries for Huma, Chi, sqlc, and TMDB leakage.
- Regenerated sqlc output and confirmed **no generated drift**.
- Ran `just check`: **all tests passed and `go vet` passed**.
- Confirmed `git diff --check` passes.

### Bottom line

The project does **not** need a layout refactor. Preserve the current module structure. The highest-value architectural work is to tighten the notes repository’s user-scoped seam and add tests at notes persistence/auth/assembly boundaries.

Your auth spans **6 files** but the real weight lands on `src/worker.ts`, which mixes four concerns that arguably don't belong together. Here's what I found, where the friction is, and ways to decompose it.

## Complexity hotspots

### 1. `worker.ts` does four jobs at once 🔴
Infrastructure binding, config assembly, auth factory construction, **and** hand-written route dispatch all live in one `Effect.gen`. The `fetch` handler is a 3-way `if/else` across Better Auth's raw handler, an inline AASA JSON response, and the Effect API.

### 2. `AuthFactory` deferred-get indirection 🔴
```ts
export interface AuthFactory {
  readonly get: Effect.Effect<Auth>;  // "resolves only inside a request"
}
```
Because `database.raw` / `email.raw` can only be resolved inside the Worker request scope, the factory defers `makeAuth()` until **every request**. A brand-new Better Auth instance is constructed on each fetch — including re-resolving raw bindings. The `as AuthFactory["get"]` cast hints at the type friction this bridge causes.

### 3. Two routers, one door 🟠
Better Auth owns `/api/auth/*` with a raw `Web Request`; Effect's `HttpApi` owns everything else. They share **no middleware, no logging, no error shape**. Auth routes bypass CORS/rate-limit/Etag layers entirely. The AASA route is a *third* special case bolted onto the same dispatcher.

### 4. Apple client-secret lives in config 🟡
`generateAppleClientSecret()` mints an ES256 JWT with a 180-day expiry, called inside `socialProviders.apple`. It's domain auth logic colocated with config wiring — and it re-signs each time Apple sign-in is used rather than caching until near-expiry.

### 5. Minor: `AuthBaseUrl` is duplicated, `TaskRepositoryLive` is unused 🟢
`AuthBaseUrl` constant in worker.ts duplicates the `AUTH_BASE_URL` config default. `TaskRepositoryLive` layer is exported but worker calls `makeTaskRepository` + `Effect.provideService` manually instead.

## The core diagnosis

Your `auth/` modules are actually well-factored — `email.ts`, `aasa.ts`, and the `BearerAuth`/`Authenticated` boundary are clean and tested. **The complexity isn't inside auth; it's the *wiring seam* between Better Auth (callback/raw-Request world) and Effect (Layer/Service world).**

`AuthFactory` is the price of that seam: Better Auth needs a raw `D1Database` resolved under the Worker's resource scope, so you defer construction per-request. That deferral forces:

- per-request Better Auth instantiation,
- a manual `path.startsWith('/api/auth/')` dispatcher living in worker.ts,
- and the Effect middleware *separately* re-calling `authFactory.get` to resolve sessions.

Fix the seam and most of the hotspots dissolve.

surfaces.markdown:
## Done — A, B, D implemented; typecheck + 14 tests green

**Approach correction worth flagging:** while implementing I found the original `AuthFactory`-as-a-*value* (not a Context service) was **intentional**, not laziness. Effect's `HttpApiMiddleware` constrains the `bearer` handler's env to route context (`Provided`), so `yield* SomeContextService` inside the middleware is rejected by the type system. My first cut used an `AuthService` Context service and the typechecker correctly rejected it (`TS2322`). I pivoted to keep the closure-passing pattern but with a memoizing `AuthServiceApi` value — same env-clean shape as before, minus the `get: Effect` indirection and per-request rebuild.

**One residual cast remains** (`getInstance as Effect<Auth>` in `runtime.ts`). It strips Alchemy's `RuntimeContext` env tag, which I verified is *residual typing only* — `database.raw` / `email.raw` are `Effect.sync(() => env[...])` reads of a captured `env` that need nothing at runtime. So the cast is honest-in-practice, and it's now consolidated into **one** place instead of at every `authFactory` construction.

## What changed per file

**`src/auth/runtime.ts`** *(new)* — `loadAuthConfig` (the 8 config reads, with `DEFAULT_AUTH_BASE_URL`), and `makeAuthService({database,email,config})` returning an `AuthServiceApi` with `getSession`/`handler`. The Better Auth instance builds **lazily on the first request** and is **memoized for the isolate lifetime** — sign-in and application routes share one instance. *(B)*

**`src/auth/config.ts`** — `makeAppleClientSecret` caches the ES256 JWT; re-signs only when < ~1 day of its 180-day lifetime remains, instead of on every Apple sign-in. `AuthSession` type moved here (lives next to `Auth`). *(D)*

**`src/auth/middleware.ts`** — `AuthFactory` interface deleted. `makeBearerAuthLive(authService: AuthServiceApi)` keeps the value-passing shape (so the middleware env stays `HttpServerRequest`-only, which `HttpApiMiddleware` accepts) but now reads `authService.getSession` instead of `authFactory.get`. *(B)*

**`src/auth/index.ts`** — exports the new runtime API; no more `AuthFactory`.

**`src/worker.ts`** — −44/+8. No config block, no factory, no `as AuthFactory["get"]` cast here, no `AuthBaseUrl` duplicate.

**`README.md`** — module map updated to list `runtime.ts`.

## Verification
- `pnpm typecheck` (tsc): ✅
- `pnpm test` (vitest + tsc): 14/14 ✅

The integration smoke tests (`pnpm test:integration`) need a deployed stage + bindings, so those remain for you to run against a dev stage when convenient.

# `seshmin`: zoxide-powered Zellij session picker

`seshmin` is a Zellij plugin that turns your zoxide history plus Zellij session state into a fast session picker.

**Core idea:**
- Show live Zellij sessions, resurrectable sessions, and frequently-used directories in one list.
- Let you fuzzy-search them.
- Switch to existing sessions or create new sessions rooted at selected directories.
- Hide sessions owned by `treemin` using the shared session registry.

# Complexity / readability review for `seshmin`

Overall: the plugin is already reasonably modular. The biggest complexity is concentrated in `State`, which currently owns event dispatch, item construction, selection behavior, search coordination, session creation, and Zellij side effects.

The best improvements are small extractions that make existing concepts explicit — not broad refactors.

flowchart TD
  A[State today] --> B[event handling]
  A --> C[item building]
  A --> D[selection movement]
  A --> E[session creation]
  A --> F[search refresh]
  A --> G[Zellij side effects]

  C:::good --> H[Extract ItemListBuilder]
  D:::good --> I[Extract selectable navigation helper]
  E:::maybe --> J[Extract session-launch helper]
  F:::easy --> K[Remove clone-based unfiltered_items]

  classDef good fill:#dff7df,stroke:#338833,color:#111;
  classDef maybe fill:#fff3cd,stroke:#997000,color:#111;

surfaces.markdown:
## Highest-value opportunities

### 1. Replace `unfiltered_items()` clone trick

**Where:** `plugins/seshmin/src/state.rs:629-657`

`unfiltered_items()` builds a partial clone of `State`, swaps in a fresh `SearchEngine`, copies session data back into it, then calls `display_items()`.

That works, but it is surprising: the reader has to understand that cloning `State` is only a workaround for `display_items()` returning search results when searching.

**Simpler shape:** split item creation from search presentation:

```rust
fn base_display_items(&self) -> Vec<SessionItem> { ... } // no search check
fn display_items(&self) -> Vec<SessionItem> {
    if self.search_engine.is_searching() { ... } else { self.base_display_items() }
}
```

Then search refresh can call `base_display_items()` directly.

**Impact:** high readability, low risk.

### 2. Extract item construction from `State`

**Where:** `plugins/seshmin/src/state.rs:154-212`

`display_items()` knows how to merge live sessions, resurrectable sessions, zoxide directories, filter them, attach rankings, format durations, and sort.

That is coherent behavior, but it makes `State` less focused. A small internal module/function could make the seam explicit:

```rust
build_display_items(
    sessions,
    resurrectable_sessions,
    directories,
    config,
    item_filter,
) -> Vec<SessionItem>
```

This would make tests for ordering/filtering independent of plugin state setup.

**Impact:** high readability/test locality, moderate risk.

### 3. Deduplicate selection movement

**Where:** `plugins/seshmin/src/state.rs:671-710` and `zoxide/search.rs`

Main selection and search selection both implement “move to next selectable item, wrapping around.” The details are duplicated across `State` and `SearchEngine`.

A small helper like this could centralize it:

```rust
fn next_selectable_index<T>(
    current: usize,
    len: usize,
    forward: bool,
    is_selectable: impl Fn(usize) -> bool,
) -> Option<usize>
```

**Impact:** medium readability, low risk.

### 4. Extract session launch/layout choice

**Where:** `plugins/seshmin/src/state.rs:472-600` approximately

`create_directory_session()` and `create_draft_session()` both decide between:

- default layout
- selected layout
- cwd-only session
- fallback when named layout is missing

This is domain logic mixed with Zellij side effects. A helper could express intent:

```rust
enum LaunchLayout { Default, Selected(usize), None }
launch_session(name, cwd, layouts, launch_layout)
```

Keep this extraction small. Avoid introducing a full abstraction unless tests need it.

**Impact:** medium readability, moderate risk.

## Lower-priority improvements

- `parse_directory(line, _config)` in `zoxide/mod.rs:31` has an unused `Config` parameter; remove it unless it is intentionally future-facing.
- `is_ignored_directory` and `is_searched_directory` duplicate path containment logic. Extract `path_is_or_descendant(path, root)`.
- `SessionManager::generate_incremented_name()` uses byte/char length inconsistently with validation. This is only a concern for non-ASCII names; either explicitly constrain to ASCII-ish names or make truncation byte-safe everywhere.
- `State::update_plugin()` could extract the `SessionUpdate` branch into `handle_session_update()` for symmetry with other event handlers.

## Recommendation

Do **not** rewrite the plugin architecture. The current shape is understandable and tested.

If improving readability, do it in this order:

1. Split `base_display_items()` from `display_items()` and delete the clone workaround.
2. Extract item building into a pure helper/module.
3. Centralize selectable-index navigation.
4. Only then consider extracting session launch/layout logic.

These keep the module deeper: callers still interact with `State`, but the implementation becomes more local and testable.

surfaces.markdown:
# 🎬 rusty-movies — a guided tour

A small Rust REST API built with the community-preferred learning stack. Over the next 5 stops we'll trace a single request from HTTP wire → router → handler → SQL → response, and call out the design tradeoffs worth knowing as a Rust learner.

## The stack

| concern | crate |
|---|---|
| web framework | **axum** 0.7 |
| async runtime | **tokio** |
| database | **sqlx** + SQLite |
| serialization | **serde** / **serde_json** |
| logging | **tracing** + tower-http TraceLayer |
| errors | **thiserror** + custom `AppError` |
| timestamps | **chrono** |

## The 4 endpoints

- `GET  /api/movies?query=…` — search the mock catalog (case-insensitive `LIKE`)
- `POST /api/watchlist { movie_id }` — save; **idempotent** (201 new / 200 existing)
- `GET  /api/watchlist` — list, joined with movie details
- `PATCH /api/watchlist/:id { watched: bool }` — mark watched, stamps `watched_at`

## How the code is laid out

```
src/
  main.rs              ← wiring: pool, migrations, router, server
  db.rs                ← pool + run_migrations
  mock_data.rs         ← seed-on-first-run dataset (8 movies)
  models.rs            ← request/response DTOs (+ sqlx::FromRow)
  error.rs             ← AppError -> IntoResponse
  handlers/
    movies.rs          ← GET /api/movies
    watchlist.rs       ← GET/POST/PATCH /api/watchlist
migrations/
  20260705000001_init.sql
```

Next stop 👉 **main.rs**, where the router is assembled.

# 🔌 main.rs — where it all gets wired together

`main.rs` does **everything up to the point a request can be served**: bring up logging, open the DB pool, run migrations, seed mock data, build the router, bind a TCP listener. The handler logic itself lives elsewhere — this file is pure assembly.

The single most important pattern to internalize here: **`#[tokio::main]` turns `main` into an async fn**, and axum handlers are *async fn*s that take their inputs as strongly-typed **extractors** (`State<...>`, `Query<...>`, `Json<...>`, `Path<...>`).

## The router — method-level routing

```rust
fn build_router(pool: SqlitePool) -> Router {
    Router::new()
        .route("/api/movies", get(handlers::movies::search_movies))
        .route(
            "/api/watchlist",
            get(handlers::watchlist::list_watchlist)
                .post(handlers::watchlist::add_to_watchlist),
        )
        .route("/api/watchlist/:id", axum::routing::patch(...))
        .with_state(pool)              // <- injected into every handler
        .layer(TraceLayer::new_for_http()) // <- request logs
}
```
Two ideas worth holding onto:

1. **`/api/watchlist` serves both GET and POST** via the chained-method API on the `MethodRouter`. One path, both verbs.
2. **`.with_state(pool)`** pushes the `SqlitePool` into the router; any handler that declares `State<SqlitePool>` as a parameter automatically receives it. That's the axum idiom for shared state.

`TraceLayer::new_for_http()` from `tower-http` produces the `DEBUG` request/response lines you saw at the end of the smoke test — free observability.

surfaces.markdown:
# 📐 models.rs + error.rs

These two files define the **contract** every request and response honors. Nothing here talks to the network — that's why axum stays clean and the handlers stay tiny.

## Request/response DTOs (`models.rs`)

```rust
#[derive(Debug, Serialize, sqlx::FromRow)]
pub struct Movie {
    pub id: i64,
    pub title: String,
    pub year: Option<i64>,
    pub director: Option<String>,
    pub genres: Option<String>,
    pub plot: Option<String>,
    pub poster_url: Option<String>,
}

#[derive(Debug, Deserialize)]
pub struct CreateWatchlistItem { pub movie_id: i64 }

#[derive(Debug, Deserialize)]
pub struct UpdateWatchlistItem { pub watched: bool }
```
- `Serialize` → outgoing JSON. `Deserialize` → incoming JSON. That's all axum needs to (de)serialize for you.
- **`sqlx::FromRow`** auto-derives "a SQL row → this struct". The rule: **column names must match field names** (so the SELECT order matters too).
- `Option<T>` maps SQL `NULL`. The mock movies have nullable `year`/`director`/etc.
- IDs are `i64` — SQLite's native integer width.

### The flat-`JOIN` shape (the design call worth knowing)

`WatchlistItem` does *not* nest a `Movie` field. Instead it's flat:

```rust
#[derive(Debug, Serialize, sqlx::FromRow)]
pub struct WatchlistItem {
    pub id: i64, pub movie_id: i64, pub watched: bool,
    pub added_at: DateTime<Utc>, pub watched_at: Option<DateTime<Utc>>,
    pub title: String, pub year: Option<i64>, // ← joined from movies
    pub director: Option<String>, pub genres: Option<String>,
    pub plot: Option<String>, pub poster_url: Option<String>,
```

# 🧭 Design tradeoffs worth remembering

These were deliberate choices, not defaults. Knowing why each was made is part of *learning the ecosystem*, not just the syntax.

## 1. Runtime `sqlx::query_as`, **not** the `query!` macro

The `sqlx::query!` / `query_as!` macros do **compile-time SQL validation** — they check your SQL against the actual schema and refuse to compile if a column doesn't exist. Amazing feature. **But** at build time they need either:
- a live DB reachable via `DATABASE_URL`, or
- a checked-in `.sqlx/` directory produced by `cargo sqlx prepare`.

For a learning project that's setup friction you don't need yet. This codebase uses the runtime API: 📜 `sqlx::query_as::<_, T>("SELECT …")`. No build-time DB needed. **You'll know you've outgrown it when** you're tired of finding typos at runtime.

**Graduation path:**
```sh
cargo install sqlx-cli
export DATABASE_URL=sqlite:./movies.db
cargo sqlx prepare   # generates .sqlx/ for offline-checked builds
```
Then swap `sqlx::query_as::<_, Movie>("SELECT …")` → `sqlx::query_as!("SELECT …")`.

## 2. WatchlistItem is **flat**, not nested

`FromRow` maps columns to fields 1-to-1. So instead of `{ movie: {...}, watched: true }`, the JSON is `{ title, year, …, watched: true }`. Took **zero** custom decoding code. The cost: the response shape is "denormalized at the API boundary", which most clients actually find more convenient anyway.

## 3. Idempotency at the SQL layer, not the handler layer

A `UNIQUE(movie_id)` constraint in the migration + `ON CONFLICT … DO NOTHING` inserts means **`POST` is safe to retry** — flaky networks can re-issue the same request without creating duplicates. We then use `rows_affected()` to report `201 Created` vs `200 OK` to the client. This is the kind of constraint that earns its keep the first time a client double-clicks "Add".

## 4. One error enum, every handler

`AppError: IntoResponse` means handlers return `AppResult<T>` and use `?`. No `match`, no `unwrap`, no `Result<_, String>` stringly-typed errors. The `#[from]` on `Sqlx` auto-converts DB errors. Adding a new error class (e.g. `BadRequest` for bad input) is one new variant + one match arm.

## 5. Seeding-on-first-run instead of fixtures

`mock_data::seed_if_empty` checks `SELECT COUNT(*) FROM movies` and only inserts if empty. You can `rm movies.db` to reseed. Keeps the mock data *in the binary*, so there's no separate fixture file to forget.

---

# 🚀 Things to try next

A small, ordered learning ladder — each is one focused step on top of what exists.

| Try | What you'll practice |
|---|---|
| Add a `DELETE /api/watchlist/:id` | Another handler shape + `DELETE FROM` |
| Add a `GET /api/movies/:id` detail route | `Path<i64>` extractor + single-row fetch (404 handling) |
| Switch one `query_as` to the `query_as!` macro | graduate to compile-time-checked SQL |
| Add `RUST_LOG=rusty_movies=debug,tower_http=trace` | explore `tracing` log filtering |
| Add a `DELETE /api/watchlist` to clear all | bulk SQL + transaction (`pool.begin().await?` … `commit().await?`) |
| Add filtering `?watched=true` to `GET /api/watchlist` | `Option<bool>` extractor param + dynamic SQL building |
| Add an integration test with `axum::TestServer` (or `reqwest`) | practice `#[tokio::test]`, in-memory `:memory:` SQLite |

---

## ✅ The whole tour, in one breath

**Request → Router (`.with_state(pool)`) → handler async fn (extractors: `State`, `Path`, `Query`, `Json`) → `sqlx` runtime query with bound `?` params → typed struct via `FromRow` → `Serialize` to JSON → response. Errors funnel through `AppError: IntoResponse` so handlers `?`-propagate. Migrations + seed-on-start live in `main`.**

That's the whole mental model. Welcome to Rust on the server — happy building. 🦀
